title: Circulatory & Nervous Systems
subtitle: Two delivery networks. One moves oxygen, the other moves information.
objectives: Name the four chambers of the heart and trace blood through both circuits
Distinguish arteries, veins and capillaries by structure and job
Name the four parts of blood and what each one does
Name the parts of the central nervous system and what each does
Describe how a neuron carries a signal
Explain a reflex arc and why it does not go through the brain

cards.title: Two systems whose whole job is delivery
cards.text: One moves oxygen and fuel. The other moves information. Both are networks, and both fail the same way — a blocked route.

cards.title: Your heart is two pumps in one case
cards.text: The right side and the left side never mix. Each one drives a different loop.
points: **Right side** → the lungs. A short, gentle loop.
**Left side** → the whole body. A long, hard one.
**Four chambers:** two atria on top, two ventricles below.
**Atria receive. Ventricles pump.**

cards.title: Trace one drop all the way round
cards.text: Four steps. Tap each one and watch the route build. Two quiz questions come from this.

question.text: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
question.explain: The right side, on a short loop. The left side does the long push to the whole body.

cards.title: Arteries, veins and capillaries
cards.text: Three kinds of vessel. The difference is the pressure each one has to survive.
points: **Arteries** carry blood *away* from the heart. Thick and elastic.
**Veins** carry it back. Thinner, with valves stopping backflow.
**Capillaries** are one cell thick. That is where exchange happens.
**A for away** is the whole memory trick.

cards.title: It is a pumped circuit, not a bucket
cards.text: A car's cooling system is a closed loop: a pump, hoses out to the radiator, hoses back. Sound familiar?
points: **The water pump** is the heart.
**The radiator** is the lungs — where the exchange happens.
**Stop the pump** and nothing else in the loop matters.
**A closed loop** means the same fluid goes round again.

question.text: What is the difference between an artery and a vein?
options: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back
Arteries carry oxygen; veins carry carbon dioxide
Arteries are in the arms; veins are in the legs
question.explain: Direction, not contents. A for artery, A for away. There is one famous exception coming.

cards.title: The one the test always asks
cards.text: Almost every artery carries oxygen-rich blood. Two vessels break that pattern, and examiners love them.
points: **Pulmonary artery:** an artery carrying oxygen-*poor* blood.
**Pulmonary vein:** a vein carrying oxygen-*rich* blood.
**Because it is going to the lungs**, not coming from them.
**Artery is about direction.** Never about oxygen.

cards.title: Four things in one liquid
cards.text: Blood is not one substance. It is cells and fragments floating in a straw-coloured liquid.
points: **Plasma** — the liquid, a bit over half of it.
**Red cells** carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
**White cells** fight infection.
**Platelets** clot a cut and stop the bleeding.

cards.title: A trained heart beats fewer times, not more
cards.text: This surprises people. Training makes the left ventricle stronger, so each single beat moves more blood.
points: **Fewer beats** are needed for the same delivery.
**A trained resting rate** can sit in the forties or fifties.
**Same adaptation as bone in Week 1.** Load it, it responds.

question.text: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
question.explain: Red cells, using haemoglobin. White cells fight infection and platelets do the clotting.

cards.title: In orbit the heart gets lazy
cards.text: On Earth your heart works against gravity to push blood upward. In orbit it does not have to.
points: **The heart muscle weakens** over a long mission.
**Exactly like bone density**, and for the same reason.
**Astronauts train daily** to stop it happening.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Delivery system done. Part 2 is the other network — the one that carries information. Your place is saved.

cards.title: The other network moves information
cards.text: Blood takes about a minute to go all the way round. A nerve signal crosses your body in a fraction of a second.

cards.title: Central and peripheral
cards.text: The nervous system splits in two. One half decides, the other reports and carries out.
points: **Central nervous system:** the brain and the spinal cord.
**Peripheral nervous system:** every nerve outside those two.
**Both are protected by bone** — skull and vertebrae.
**Week 1 said the skeleton protects.** This is what it protects.

cards.title: One neuron, four parts
cards.text: A neuron is a cell built to carry a signal in one direction only.
points: **Dendrites** receive the incoming signal.
**The axon** carries it away, sometimes a metre long.
**Myelin** wraps the axon and makes the signal much faster.
**The synapse** is the gap where one neuron passes to the next.

question.text: What makes up the central nervous system?
options: The brain and the spinal cord
The brain and all the nerves
The spinal cord and the muscles
question.explain: Brain and spinal cord. Everything else is the peripheral nervous system.

cards.title: Your nerves outrun the car
cards.text: A myelinated motor nerve can carry a signal at around 120 metres per second.
points: **That is over 400 kilometres an hour.**
**Faster than a Formula 1 car flat out.**
**Strip the myelin off** and the signal crawls.
**Insulation is the speed.** Same as a good cable.

cards.title: Three parts, three jobs
cards.text: The brain is not one lump. The exam wants three regions and what each one runs.
points: **Cerebrum** — thinking, memory, decisions, voluntary movement.
**Cerebellum** — balance, coordination, timing.
**Brain stem** — breathing and heart rate, without asking you.
**You cannot decide to stop your brain stem.**

cards.title: Death Stranding put the cerebellum on screen
cards.text: That game makes you feel every shift in the load. Your cerebellum does the same job constantly, for free.
points: **Carrying a heavy pack** shifts your centre of gravity.
**The cerebellum corrects it** before you notice.
**Damage it** and walking becomes a conscious task.

question.text: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
question.explain: The cerebellum. The cerebrum thinks, and the brain stem runs breathing and heart rate.

cards.title: Tap through a reflex
cards.text: Hand on a hot pan. Four steps, and the last one is the surprise.

cards.title: The brain is told afterwards
cards.text: A reflex skips the brain because the brain is too slow for this. Damage happens in milliseconds.
points: **Sensory neuron in, motor neuron out.**
**One relay in the spinal cord** connects them.
**You feel the pain** after your hand has already moved.
**That gap is the reflex doing its job.**

cards.title: Slipping a punch is not a reflex
cards.text: People call it one, but it goes through the brain. That is exactly why it takes years of practice.
points: **A true reflex** is wired in. You are born with it.
**A trained reaction** is learned, and it gets faster.
**Which is why sparring works** and reading about it does not.

question.text: In a reflex, the signal reaches your brain before your muscle moves.
question.explain: False. The spinal cord handles it. You feel the pain after your hand has already gone.

terms.def: An upper chamber of the heart. It receives blood. Two of them: right and left.
A lower chamber of the heart. It pumps blood out. The left one has the thickest wall.
A vessel carrying blood away from the heart. Thick and elastic.
A vessel carrying blood back to the heart. Thinner, with valves.
The smallest vessel, one cell thick. Where oxygen and waste are exchanged.
The substance in red blood cells that oxygen attaches to.
The straw-coloured liquid the blood cells float in. A bit over half of blood.
The brain and the spinal cord. Everything else is peripheral.
A nerve cell. Dendrites in, axon out, synapse at the far end.
The insulating sheath around an axon. It makes the signal far faster.
Sensory neuron, spinal relay, motor neuron. It does not go via the brain.
The part of the brain that handles balance, coordination and timing.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Right side to the lungs. Left side to the body.**
**Arteries away, veins back, capillaries exchange.**
**Central nervous system = brain plus spinal cord.**
**A reflex skips the brain.** That is the whole point.

quiz.text: Put these in the order blood travels through them.
quiz.explain: Body in on the right, out to the lungs, back in on the left, out to the body again.
quiz.objective: Name the four chambers of the heart and trace blood through both circuits

quiz.text: Which chamber has the thickest muscular wall, and why?
options: The left ventricle, because it pumps to the whole body
The right ventricle, because it pumps to the lungs
The left atrium, because it receives from the lungs
The right atrium, because it receives from the body
quiz.explain: The left ventricle. It is the longest, hardest push in the system, so it needs the most muscle.
quiz.objective: Name the four chambers of the heart and trace blood through both circuits

options: It carries blood away from the heart
It is always found close to the skin
quiz.explain: Direction, not contents. The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood and is still an artery.
quiz.objective: Distinguish arteries, veins and capillaries by structure and job

quiz.text: Where does the exchange of oxygen and waste actually happen?
quiz.explain: Capillaries. Their walls are one cell thick, which is what makes exchange possible.
quiz.objective: Distinguish arteries, veins and capillaries by structure and job

quiz.text: The pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood.
quiz.explain: True. It is heading to the lungs to collect oxygen, so it has not picked any up yet.
quiz.objective: Distinguish arteries, veins and capillaries by structure and job

quiz.text: What substance in red blood cells does oxygen attach to?
quiz.explain: Haemoglobin. It is what makes red blood cells red, and what lets them carry oxygen.
quiz.objective: Name the four parts of blood and what each one does

quiz.text: Which part of the blood stops a cut from bleeding?
quiz.explain: Platelets. They clump together and form the clot. White cells fight infection instead.
quiz.objective: Name the four parts of blood and what each one does

quiz.text: What are the two parts of the central nervous system?
options: The brain and the spinal cord
The spinal cord and the nerves
The brain and the sense organs
quiz.explain: Brain and spinal cord, both protected by bone. Every other nerve is peripheral.
quiz.objective: Name the parts of the central nervous system and what each does

quiz.text: Which brain part keeps you breathing without you thinking about it?
quiz.explain: The brain stem. It runs breathing and heart rate, and you cannot switch it off on purpose.
quiz.objective: Name the parts of the central nervous system and what each does

options: It insulates the axon so the signal travels much faster
It receives signals from other neurons
It is the gap between two neurons
It carries oxygen to the nerve cell
quiz.explain: It insulates. A myelinated nerve can carry a signal at about 120 metres per second.
quiz.objective: Describe how a neuron carries a signal

quiz.text: Put a reflex in order, from touching a hot pan onward.
items: Sensory neuron carries the signal in
Motor neuron makes the muscle move
quiz.explain: The brain is last. Your hand has already moved by the time you feel anything.
quiz.objective: Explain a reflex arc and why it does not go through the brain

quiz.text: Why does a reflex not go through the brain first?
options: Going via the brain would be too slow to prevent damage
The brain cannot control muscles at all
The brain is asleep most of the time
Reflexes only happen in the legs
quiz.explain: Speed. Damage happens in milliseconds, so the spinal cord decides and tells the brain afterwards.
quiz.objective: Explain a reflex arc and why it does not go through the brain

teacher.summary: Week 5 Science covers the circulatory and nervous systems together, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. The two are taught as the same kind of thing — a delivery network — so the second half has a structure to hang on rather than starting from nothing. Two interactive figures carry the parts that a paragraph handles badly: the double circulation loop, and the reflex arc where the ordering is the whole lesson. The reflex figure deliberately ends on the brain being informed last, because that is the point students most often get backwards. Two callbacks to Week 1 are built in: bone as protection for the central nervous system, and training adaptation applied to the heart.
discussion: Ask him why the left ventricle is thicker than the right. If he can answer from the loop lengths rather than from memory, he has understood the double circuit.
Ask him to explain the pulmonary artery to you. It is the fastest way to find out whether 'artery' means direction or oxygen in his head.
Ask what would happen if the reflex arc did go through the brain. It turns a memorised sequence into a reason.
Ask him to name something his cerebellum did in the last minute. Sitting upright counts, and that is the surprise.
teacher.extension: Have him take his own resting pulse for one minute, then again after twenty burpees, then once a minute until it comes back down. The recovery curve is the interesting part, and it is his own data rather than a textbook's.
misconceptions: 'Arteries carry oxygen, veins carry carbon dioxide.' Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The pulmonary artery is oxygen-poor and the pulmonary vein is oxygen-rich.
'The heart pumps blood around one big circle.' There are two circuits, and the two sides of the heart never mix.
'A reflex is a fast decision by the brain.' The brain is not involved in making it. The spinal cord relays it and the brain is told afterwards.
'Slipping a punch is a reflex.' It is a trained response that goes through the brain, which is why it takes years to learn.
